metadata.title: Exoplanet Hunting: Teaching AI to Show Its Work
metadata.purpose: Weekly STEM explainer Ep.02: a deep-dive on AI exoplanet vetting that goes past Ep.01's AstroNet/Kepler-90i story. Covers the three false-positive types that fake a transit signal, then NASA Ames's ExoMiner (2021) - a classifier built from separate, explainable diagnostic-test branches (centroid offset, odd-even, secondary eclipse) that validated 301 Kepler planets in one pass and was later extended as ExoMiner++ to screen TESS's ongoing candidate stream. Source: weekly_stem_videos/ideas.md, Astronomy section, topic 02 'Exoplanet hunting.' Authored 2026-08-01; built and rendered to a 4K master the same day. Rebuilt 2026-08-01 to insert a new presenter self-introduction/executive-summary beat as B02 (mirroring the same insertion made to Ep.01), pushing every former B02-B19 beat to B03-B20.
metadata.clock: narration (Kokoro af_heart) - durations are MEASURED actual audio, not estimates. All 20 beats have measured actual_duration_s.
metadata.color_semantics: TEAL = signal/confirmed/real planet; CRIMSON = noise/false-positive/impostor; never swapped mid-film
metadata.note: New project, authored from scratch 2026-08-01; rebuilt same day to add a presenter self-introduction beat (B02). Deliberately does not reuse Ep.01's AstroNet dual-view mechanism or the Kepler-90i case (per Ep.01 README's own guidance for a follow-up episode). Zero real-archive stills and zero paid generation by design - every GRAPHIC beat is an original Manim diagram and every CARD beat is an original Remotion SlateCard, so no photo-rights research was needed (see PROMPTS.md). Rebuilt 2026-08-01 (second pass): swapped B01/B02 order so the presenter intro ('Hi, I'm Om Mali...') now opens the film, followed by the original cold-open hook ('By 2021, thousands of Kepler's flagged...').

beats.narration_text: Hi, I'm Om Mali. This video is about how NASA built an AI system that explains exactly why it thinks a signal is a real planet, instead of just giving a yes or no answer.

shot.note: NEW 2026-08-01. Presenter self-introduction / executive summary card, inserted as beat 2 right after the cold open. Not a factual claim beat - see FACTCHECK.md. Matches the WELCOME-eyebrow convention used for ai-vs-the-data-deluge's own intro card for series consistency.

beats.narration_text: By 2021, thousands of Kepler's flagged 'maybe' signals were still sitting unconfirmed.

shot.note: COLD OPEN. A dense grid of small light-curve tiles, all the same muted slate color - a visual 'backlog,' no single signal highlighted yet (deliberately unresolved, unlike Ep.01's single-highlight open).

beats.narration_text: Not because anyone missed them. It's because 'maybe' takes real proof to become 'yes.'

shot.note: COLD OPEN title/thesis card.

beats.narration_text: A dip in a star's brightness can come from three different impostors. It doesn't have to be a planet.

shot.note: One clean light curve with a dip, then three labeled branch-lines fanning out from it toward three icon placeholders (to be named in the next three beats).

beats.narration_text: The first impostor is an eclipsing binary. That's a pair of two stars orbiting each other, and when one passes in front of the other, it creates a dip that looks just like a planet crossing a single star.

shot.note: Two-star icon eclipsing, producing a light curve with a matching dip PLUS a faint secondary dip elsewhere in the orbit.

beats.narration_text: The second impostor is stellar variability. That's when a star dims on its own, with no planet or companion star involved, often because of starspots or flares.

shot.note: A single star icon with a wandering, irregular brightness curve (no clean periodic dip - jittery, spot-driven wobble).

beats.narration_text: The third impostor isn't a real signal at all. It's an instrumental artifact caused by the camera itself.

shot.note: A light curve with a sharp, jagged glitch-like dip rendered in a visibly different (angular, non-organic) line style than the two real astrophysical curves above.

beats.narration_text: Three impostors, one signal. Telling them apart took specialist time nobody had to spare.

props.headline: Three impostors, one signal - and specialist time nobody had to spare.

shot.note: Act-closing summary card.

beats.narration_text: In 2021, NASA's Ames Research Center built a different kind of classifier called ExoMiner.

props.headline: NASA Ames, 2021: a different kind of classifier - ExoMiner.

shot.note: THE TURN title/name card - text only, no likeness of any named individual (see FACTCHECK.md).

beats.narration_text: It doesn't just scan the light curve. It runs the same diagnostic tests a human vetter would.

shot.note: One light curve at top splitting into several parallel labeled branch-lines below it, each branch ending in an empty checkbox (to be filled in the next three beats).

beats.narration_text: Each test becomes its own branch of the network, checked separately before anything is decided.

shot.note: The branch diagram from B09 relabeled with the three named tests (centroid, odd-even, secondary eclipse), each branch now shown as its own small convolutional block.

beats.narration_text: One branch checks the centroid. It asks whether the dip's light really comes from this star, or from a neighboring star sneaking in.

shot.note: A target star with a faint neighboring star nearby; a highlighted centroid marker shifts slightly toward the neighbor during the dip, flagged in CRIMSON.

beats.narration_text: Another branch compares odd numbered and even numbered transits. A real planet repeats identically every time, but an eclipsing binary often doesn't.

shot.note: Two small stacked light-curve panels, 'odd transits' and 'even transits' - matching depths in TEAL for the planet case, mismatched depths in CRIMSON for the binary case.

beats.narration_text: A third branch hunts for a second, shallower dip. That's the signature of a hidden stellar companion.

shot.note: A full-orbit phase-folded light curve with the main transit dip plus a small secondary dip elsewhere, the secondary dip highlighted with a HandRing in CRIMSON.

beats.narration_text: Only after every branch reports back does the network merge them into one explainable verdict.

shot.note: Synthesis beat - three labeled branch chips (centroid, odd-even, secondary eclipse) each feeding an arrow into one merge node, which outputs a single verdict chip. Mirrors Ep.01's B11 synthesis shot, but with three inputs instead of two.

beats.narration_text: At 99% precision, it recovered 93.6% of real planets. The previous best classifier caught just 76.3%.

props.headline: 99% precision, 93.6% recall - vs. 76.3% for the prior best classifier

shot.note: Stat overlay: precision/recall comparison.

beats.narration_text: In a single pass through Kepler's unconfirmed backlog, it validated 301 new exoplanets at once.

props.headline: 301 new exoplanets validated in a single batch

shot.note: Stat overlay: 301-planet batch validation, Astrophysical Journal, Feb 2022.

beats.narration_text: By 2026, the same diagnostic branch design was extended as ExoMiner Plus Plus, and it was screening TESS's ongoing candidate stream too.

props.headline: ExoMiner++ (2026): the same design, now screening TESS

shot.note: Transition card into the scaling-up beat.

beats.narration_text: It flagged 7,330 likely planets among more than 147,000 unconfirmed TESS signals.

props.headline: 7,330 flagged candidates out of 147,000+ TESS signals

shot.note: Stat counter.

beats.narration_text: This AI doesn't just say yes or no anymore. It shows exactly which test convinced it.

props.headline: It doesn't just say yes or no. It shows exactly which test convinced it.

shot.note: Closing title/text card.
